transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-30 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~64 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SRE), Tom Ruiz (Sable Platform Eng), Aisha Khan (Sable ML Infra Lead), Ben Ortiz (Sable SRE), Maya Patel (CTO)

Summary:
Quick technical deep-dive focused on handling peaky traffic for Sable Health's on-prem inference cluster. Primary goals: reduce p99 latency during bursts, maximize steady-state throughput, and keep token-unit cost predictable while staying within compliance constraints for PHI. Covered continuous-batching behavior, fair-queueing vs strict priority windows, prefetch/prewarm strategies for KV cache, max_num_seqs tradeoffs, and token limits/guardrails. Agreed on a pilot to run continuous-batching with conservative max_num_seqs and prewarm on a dedicated 4-GPU node.

Topics:
- Continuous batching and its latency-throughput curve
- Fair queueing / slot allocation for tenants and priority windows
- max_num_seqs and token ceiling effects on throughput
- KV cache prewarm, eviction, hit-rate measurement
- Quantization impacts on GPU memory / max sequences
- VPC/on-prem constraints and network cold starts

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena Ortiz: all right hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll get started, uh this is Lena from Redwood, uh Marcus is on the SE side, Priya is on SRE ops. Tom, Aisha, Ben, Maya from Sable, thanks for taking the time. We're going to focus on throughput strategies for peaky loads on your on-prem setup.
[00:15] Tom Ruiz: yep thanks, uh just to set context we run intermittant bursts, like 10x for 30-90s, usually tied to batch ingestion pipelines, and we're seeing p99 spikes up to 2.1s which breaks user SLAs.
[00:32] Marcus Chen: right, so common... and you mentioned you're on a pinned VPC on-prem deployment, right? that means we can control prewarm behavior and KV cache persistence which helps a lot.
[00:44] Aisha Khan: correct, we have a 4-GPU pool, A100-ish, though it's slightly older cards, and we need to keep everything inside the air-gapped network for PHI. so cloud burst isn't an option.
[00:58] Marcus Chen: understood. two big levers I want our discussion to revolve around: scheduler knobs (windowing, slot sizes, fairness weights) and model-level limits (max_num_seqs, token caps, quantization profiles). these interact with the continuous-batching runtime heavily.
[01:15] Ben Ortiz: when you say "slot sizes" is that per-request token window or per-sequence slot? we've been tuning batch size but not slots specifically.
[01:26] Marcus Chen: good question. in our runtime a "slot" maps to a scheduling window that can accept up to N seqs concurrently; it's related to batch packing heuristics. increasing slot size allows more seq packing but increases head-of-line blocking risk.
[01:41] Maya Patel: head-of-line blocking is the issue; during bursts we get one or two big requests that make small interactive calls wait.
[01:48] Marcus Chen: exactly. two approaches: fair-queueing where each tenant or priority class gets a quota of slots per window, or priority windows that reserve a small fraction for low-latency interactive queries. fair-queueing tends to be smoother overall but can be slightly less optimal in peak throughput.
[02:03] Tom Ruiz: Can you expand on the tradeoff with max_num_seqs? our current config uses a high value, 128, to maximize throughput.
[02:12] Marcus Chen: sure. max_num_seqs controls the number of sequences the GPU will keep in-flight for KV cache and attention memory. high max_num_seqs improves GPU utilization but increases per-request latency and memory pressure; it also makes cold-start misses more costly because the kv cache needs to be populated for more sequences. with older A100s you may hit memory fragmentation and paging if quantization isn't aggressively used.
[02:36] Aisha Khan: so are we better lowering max_num_seqs and relying on continuous batching to drive throughput?
[02:42] Marcus Chen: often yes for peaky patterns. a conservative strategy: reduce max_num_seqs to 32 or 48 for interactive paths, keep a separate lane for batch ingestion with max_num_seqs 96-128. then use routing rules to send interactive traffic to low-latency lane. that's where fair-queueing or token buckets come in.
[02:59] Lena Ortiz: quick note - routing rules can be policy based in Redwood console, e.g. header-based route to low-latency pool. we'll share an example.
[03:08] [00:03:08] Tom Ruiz: the KV cache question: our hit-rate is erratic after downtimes; can we prewarm?
[03:17] Marcus Chen: yes, KV cache prewarm is supported on private deployments. two practical methods: 1) proactive prefix prewarm using a warmup trace (replay common prefixes), or 2) reactive warm-up where first request triggers async prefetch for that session while returning a partial response then finishing streamed tokens. prewarming needs persistent cache across requests - ensure the process that owns the cache isn't being restarted during autoscaler cycles.
[03:42] Ben Ortiz: hmm we do have autoscaler set to aggressively downscale when idle, which kills cache.
[03:47] Priya Nair: that's a common misconfig. perhaps set a small idle-reserve and prefer soft downscale + prewarm script.
[03:54] Marcus Chen: exactly, you can set a soft pool with 1 reserved slot to keep the cache hot. combined with prewarm traces you get high KV hit-rate at burst start.
[04:05] [00:04:05] Aisha Khan: about eviction policies, is LRU always best? our workloads have a mix of long-lived sessions and many short queries.
[04:15] Marcus Chen: LRU is simple but not always ideal. we often recommend a segmented eviction: keep a protected set for long-lived session keys and a probabilistic discard for ephemeral sequences. Redwood runtime supports a hotset threshold and a small protected window for sticky sessions. that reduces re-warming cost for long sessions.
[04:33] Tom Ruiz: what about metrics we should collect to prove improvements?
[04:36] Marcus Chen: p50/p95/p99 latency by route, kv cache hit-rate, prewarm success rate, GPU mem usage, scheduler slot occupancy, batch packing efficiency, and token-cost per request. instrument at token level if possible.
[04:52] [00:04:52] Maya Patel: ok, can you walk through an example config you recommend for our 4-GPU on-prem environment?
[05:01] Marcus Chen: sure, high level: dedicate two GPUs as low-latency lane (max_num_seqs=32, slot_size small, priority windows enabled), two GPUs as high-throughput lane (max_num_seqs=96-128, slot_size larger). set fair weights 60/40 low-latency:throughput, enable kv-cache persistent on the low-latency lane, prewarm traces run 2 minutes before expected bursts if schedule-known.
[05:27] Tom Ruiz: our bursts are somewhat predictable but not always scheduled. how does an adaptive approach look?
[05:33] Marcus Chen: adaptive: measure incoming RPS trend; if RPS derivative exceeds threshold, temporarily shift weights using sliding window. also scale a small burst pool (ephemeral GPUs) if available in your data center. but since you're air-gapped, ephemeral may be limited. more realistic: keep a hot small reserved pool for bursts.
[05:52] [00:05:52] Ben Ortiz: latency tail is our main SLA risk. how do token limits / caps help here?
[05:58] Marcus Chen: token caps per-request enforce an upper bound on expensive requests. you can enforce two layers: per-request token ceiling and per-tenant token burn rate. if a request exceeds a threshold, reroute to lower-priority lane or reject. this prevents single large requests from starving interactive ones.
[06:16] Aisha Khan: we worry about user features that generate long outputs for clinical notes. can't just cap tokens bluntly.
[06:23] Marcus Chen: you can implement graduated caps based on route type—clinical-notes route gets higher cap but runs on throughput lane; interactive chat has strict low cap and uses low-latency lane. also consider partial streaming and progressive decoding so interactive can return partial answers quickly.
[06:39] [00:06:39] Lena Ortiz: there's also quantization effects to consider; we know Sable uses some int8 profiles in staging. Marcus?
[06:45] Marcus Chen: quantization reduces memory per-activation so allows higher max_num_seqs or larger batch packing, but it can change latency characteristics slightly and sometimes increase jitter; it also affects model quality. with INT8 you might safely push throughput lane to max_num_seqs 160 on larger GPUs, but test for hallucination/regression. we'll run eval traces.
[07:03] Tom Ruiz: is there a quick experiment you recommend to measure safe quantized max_num_seqs?
[07:08] Marcus Chen: yes: controlled sweep—run short 10-minute trials with increasing max_num_seqs (32, 48, 64, 96, 128) while streaming the same workload and measuring p99 and GPU mem usage. check quality regression at each step with sample prompts. Redwood has a benchmarking harness we'll share.
[07:25] [00:07:25] Aisha Khan: about the scheduler knobs: can you name the exact knobs we should change? I've seen window_ms, slot_capacity, max_batch_tokens, and fairness_weight in the console.
[07:35] Marcus Chen: the names vary by runtime version but the conceptual knobs are: window_ms (duration of scheduling window), slot_capacity (max sequences per slot), slot_memory_limit (enforces memory-based ceilings), fairness_weight (per-class weight), prefetch_workers (concurrency for kv prefetch), and max_num_seqs at model shim. Changing window_ms from 100ms to 50ms reduces batching latency but can reduce packing efficiency — a classic trade.
[07:56] [00:07:56] Ben Ortiz: if we reduce window_ms we might need to increase scheduler loop frequency which adds CPU overhead, correct?
[08:02] Marcus Chen: yes, there's CPU scheduling cost. on small on-prem nodes check scheduler loop CPU usage; you might need to bump the control-plane SLO for the node.
[08:10] Tom Ruiz: any thoughts on fair-queueing algorithms — deficit round robin vs weighted fair queueing?
[08:16] Marcus Chen: DRR is simpler and works well when requests are similar; WFQ gives stronger theoretical fairness and better for variable sized requests. for mixed short/long patterns WFQ with token buckets per class tends to reduce starvations.
[08:29] [00:08:29] Maya Patel: are there existing Redwood presets for healthcare that are a good starting point?
[08:36] Lena Ortiz: yes, we have a "compliance-sensitive low-latency" preset and a "throughput heavy" preset; we'll attach the starter presets to the follow-up email.
[08:45] Marcus Chen: another tip: use soft token ceilings that trigger a graceful fallback to compressed model variant (quantized or smaller model) before outright rejection. this gives continuity.
[08:58] [00:08:58] Aisha Khan: our ops team is nervous about autoscaler downscales killing the cache. besides reserve pool what else?
[09:04] Priya Nair: instrument an eviction trace and alert when downscale correlates with KV miss spike; plus add a short-lived sticky session that periodically pings to keep one worker alive during idle periods.
[09:13] Marcus Chen: and ensure KMS/HSM token refresh isn't a hidden restart cause — we've seen agents that refresh keys and fully restart processes.
[09:22] [00:09:22] Tom Ruiz: on the monitoring front, what dashboards should we set up first for the pilot?
[09:28] Marcus Chen: start with p99 latency per-route, kv-cache hit-rate, scheduler slot utilization, batch packing efficiency (avg seqs per batch), GPU mem headroom, and token-units per minute. also track quality regression via small eval set.
[09:45] [00:09:45] Lena Ortiz: ok let's pivot to an example failure mode and mitigation sequence — say a cold restart during peak that leads to cold kv miss storm.
[09:54] Marcus Chen: mitigation recipe: detect sudden kv-hit drop + p99 spike, immediately route new requests to a small cold-fallback model variant (smaller quantized model) while spinning up an emergency prewarm job to repopulate caches. also temporarily reduce max_num_seqs to avoid memory thrashing. once hit-rate recovers, shift traffic back.
[10:16] [00:10:16] Ben Ortiz: would the fallback model need separate deployment artifacts or can it be an alternate model version in same pool?
[10:23] Marcus Chen: can be deployed as a variant in the same model catalog; Redwood routing can swap to that variant by policy. that's preferable to stand-up a new deployment for speed.
[10:33] [00:10:33] Aisha Khan: what about testing these transitions automatically?
[10:37] Marcus Chen: we recommend chaos-style tests: intentionally kill a worker, then measure failover time, p99 uplift, and recovery. run these in staging before production.
[10:47] [00:10:47] Maya Patel: let's talk numbers: if we move to the two-lane approach you suggested, what p99 reduction is realistic?
[10:55] Marcus Chen: customers typically see p99 drop from 2s to ~400-700ms for interactive lane on similar hardware with reserved cache and prewarm. throughput lane might have slightly worse p99 but overall throughput increases. exact numbers depend on model size, quantization, and seq lengths.
[11:14] [00:11:14] Tom Ruiz: about policy routing, can we do dynamic tagging per request so our app decides lane?
[11:19] Lena Ortiz: yes header-based or token-based routing is common, even sampling rules. we'll share examples.
[11:26] [00:11:26] Aisha Khan: one more thing — are there legal risks with persistent caches for PHI? we need to ensure KV cache data residency and encryption.
[11:34] Marcus Chen: KV cache stores intermediate activations; in on-prem deployments data never leaves your network and we integrate with your KMS/HSM for encryption at rest. the main risk is persistent logs or debug traces — ensure redaction and retention policies. Redwood can turn off remote telemetry for Private deployments.
[11:54] [00:11:54] Ben Ortiz: thanks, that's reassuring.
[12:00] [00:12:00] Lena Ortiz: ok let's sketch the pilot timeline: Aisha to provision test node by Apr 1, Redwood to provide configs and scripts, run pilot Apr 6 week, then sync Apr 10 for results.
[12:11] Aisha Khan: yes we'll try to hit those dates.
[12:15] [00:12:15] Tom Ruiz: any gotchas on on-prem GPU drivers or NCCL versions? we've struggled before with older NCCL and patched kernels.
[12:23] Marcus Chen: ensure drivers match Redwood's validated matrix — older NCCL may cause kernel fallbacks that kill perf. we'll include a validation checklist. also confirm CUDA, cuDNN versions, MIG config if using A100 VMs.
[12:36] [00:12:36] Maya Patel: we do not use MIG. whole card per container.
[12:40] Marcus Chen: that simplifies memory accounting but requires careful slot_memory_limit settings.
[12:46] [00:12:46] Aisha Khan: on the prewarm script — do you have a way to generate warm traces without replaying real PHI? we need synthetic but representative prompts.
[12:54] Marcus Chen: yes, Redwood has a synthetic trace generator that preserves token length distribution and prefix patterns without actual content; it's privacy-safe. we'll share and can seed with anonymized templates.
[13:07] [00:13:07] Ben Ortiz: since our node pool is small, is there a risk prewarm itself creates a burst that degrades service?
[13:14] Marcus Chen: keep prewarm at low concurrency and schedule it just ahead of expected peaks; or use background prefetch workers with rate limits so it doesn't compete with foreground traffic. prewarm can also run on throughput lane to avoid interfering.
[13:28] [00:13:28] Tom Ruiz: any final remarks on token limits and billing predictability?
[13:33] Marcus Chen: token rate limits per-tenant and per-route give you predictability. combine them with fair-queueing and throttles that return standard error codes so app can backoff gracefully. we can also provide token-cost estimates from recent traces so you can model monthly burn under various patterns.
[13:49] [00:13:49] Lena Ortiz: great, we're near the end; quick recap of concrete next steps.
[13:54] Marcus Chen: recap: 1) Redwood sends scheduler cookbook, presets, benchmarks harness, and prewarm scripts. 2) Sable provisions 4-GPU test node, sets small reserved pool and agrees to run pilot week of Apr 6. 3) Run controlled param sweep on max_num_seqs and quant levels and report p99 and quality.
[14:14] Tom Ruiz: ok we'll aim for that. thanks.
[14:18] Maya Patel: thanks everyone.
[14:20] [00:14:20] Lena Ortiz: thanks all, we'll follow up with email and attach configs. bye.

End of meeting.
